charts.title: Automotive & Life Sciences Segment Revenue
charts.annotation: Corning restructured reporting segments in 2026 (Optical Communications, Glass Innovations, Automotive, Solar, Life Sciences & Emerging Growth Businesses). Only the two segments that kept a stable definition across the change -- Automotive and the legacy Life Sciences line -- are promoted to the CSV; Optical Communications, Glass Innovations and Solar are tracked in the kpis table but not yet charted here.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Corning Incorporated: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Corning Incorporated: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Corning Incorporated: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Corning Incorporated: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Corning Incorporated: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Corning Incorporated: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Corning Incorporated: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Corning Incorporated: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
Corning reports revenue by operating segment. Automotive (glass and ceramic substrates for emissions and connected-vehicle electronics) and the legacy Life Sciences segment (lab glassware and plastics) kept consistent definitions through Corning's 2026 segment reorganisation, unlike the other lines.

For Corning Incorporated: the far larger story is Optical Communications, which the 2026 layout keeps as its own segment and which carries the AI-datacenter fiber demand (including the ~$6bn multi-year Meta deal under the "Springboard" plan) -- it is not yet a promoted CSV column, so it is absent from this chart even though it is the single biggest driver of the revenue line above. Glass Innovations (the 2026 merger of the old Display and Specialty Materials segments) and Solar are newer still and only populated in a handful of recent quarters.

What to watch:

  • Automotive revenue tracking global light-vehicle production and the EV/ICE mix (glass substrates sell into both)
  • Life Sciences as a steady, low-growth base business funding the Optical Communications buildout
  • Segment definitions are not comparable before vs after the 2026 restructure -- do not read a step-change here as organic growth or decline

coreEps.title: Core (non-GAAP) EPS
coreEps.content:
Core EPS is Corning's own adjusted earnings measure: GAAP EPS with restructuring, discrete tax items, and other items management deems non-operating added back. Reported EPS is unadjusted GAAP.

For Corning Incorporated: Corning guides and is judged by Core EPS, not GAAP EPS -- the gap has been meaningful in restructuring-heavy years (e.g. the Display/Specialty Materials-to-Glass Innovations transition), so the two lines should be read together rather than Core EPS alone.

What to watch:

  • A widening Core-vs-GAAP gap that persists for several years (recurring "one-offs" are not one-off)
  • Core EPS growth versus the Springboard plan's stated targets

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Corning Incorporated: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
